result.markdown: --- course-unit: ch14-advanced-optimal-control status: complete --- # Advanced optimal control {#sec-advanced-optimal-control} ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} **Self-study**: not taught at the workshop, but complete and ready to use on your own. ::: @sec-interventions-and-optimization optimised a *finite* set of intervention parameters — when to start a lockdown, how long to hold it — around an ODE simulation. This chapter treats the intervention itself as an unknown **function** of time. Nothing constrains the policy to be a step; the solver is free to return whatever shape minimises the objective, and the shape it returns is informative. The chapter follows the formulations collected in [EpiPolicies](https://github.com/epirecipes/EpiPolicies): minimising cases under a resource budget, holding prevalence beneath a capacity threshold, and combining a non-pharmaceutical intervention with vaccination. ## Learning goals You will: - state a continuous-time optimal control problem and discretise it by collocation; - read the shape of an optimal policy rather than only its objective value; - impose a **path constraint** and see what it costs; - combine two controls with different mechanisms and budgets; and - distinguish a binding constraint from a slack one, and both from infeasibility. ## Model assumptions and classification The controlled model is the SIR system of @sec-ordinary-differential-equations in proportions, with $S(0)=0.99$, $I(0)=0.01$, $\beta c = 0.5$ and $\gamma = 0.25$, so $R_0 = 2$. It stays **deterministic, continuous-time, continuous-state and population-level**; what is new is that some coefficients are decision variables rather than parameters. Two controls appear. A non-pharmaceutical intervention $u(t) \in [0, u_{\max}]$ reduces transmission by the factor $1-u(t)$, and is *costly to sustain*, so its time integral is bounded by a budget $B$. A vaccination rate $v(t) \in [0, v_{\max}]$ moves susceptibles directly to immunity, and is limited by a total supply $V$. The distinction matters: $u$ suppresses transmission only while it is applied, whereas $v$ permanently removes susceptibles. ## Equations The controlled dynamics, with cumulative incidence $C$ tracked for the objective: $$ \begin{aligned} \dot S(t) &= -(1-u(t))\,\beta c\,S(t)I(t) - v(t)S(t),\\ \dot I(t) &= (1-u(t))\,\beta c\,S(t)I(t)-\gamma I(t),\\ \dot C(t) &= (1-u(t))\,\beta c\,S(t)I(t). \end{aligned} $$ {#eq-ch14-controlled-sir} The base problem minimises final cumulative incidence with a small quadratic regulariser, which discourages the numerically awkward chattering that an unregularised bang-bang solution can produce: $$ \begin{aligned} \underset{S,I,C,u}{\operatorname{minimize}}\quad & C(t_f) + 10^{-3}\int_0^{t_f}u(t)^2\,\mathrm dt\\ \text{subject to}\quad & 0\le u(t)\le u_{\max},\qquad \int_0^{t_f}u(t)\,\mathrm dt\le B . \end{aligned} $$ {#eq-ch14-objective} Two extensions follow. A **path constraint** $$ I(t) \le I_{\max} \qquad \text{for all } t $$ {#eq-ch14-path} expresses finite hospital capacity: it constrains the trajectory at every instant, not merely at the end. And a **second control** adds the vaccination terms of @eq-ch14-controlled-sir with $\int_0^{t_f} v(t)\,\mathrm dt \le V$. Because $u$ is a function, the problem is infinite-dimensional. Collocation replaces it with a finite nonlinear program by representing each variable on a grid of supports and enforcing the dynamics there. ## Julia implementation One builder covers all three problems, so the comparisons that follow differ only in the arguments passed. ::: {#cell-code-ch14-builder .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using CairoMakie using InfiniteOpt using Ipopt const tf = 20.0 const βc = 0.5 const γ = 0.25 function control_problem(; umax = 0.5, budget = 2.0, capacity = nothing, vaccination = false, vmax = 0.05, supply = 0.4, n_supports = 41) model = InfiniteModel(Ipopt.Optimizer) set_optimizer_attribute(model, "print_level", 0) set_optimizer_attribute(model, "max_iter", 3000) set_optimizer_attribute(model, "tol", 1e-7) @infinite_parameter(model, t in [0.0, tf], num_supports = n_supports, derivative_method = OrthogonalCollocation(2)) @variable(model, S >= 0, Infinite(t), start = 0.99) @variable(model, I >= 0, Infinite(t), start = 0.01) @variable(model, C >= 0, Infinite(t), start = 0.0) @variable(model, 0 <= u <= umax, Infinite(t), start = 0.0) @constraint(model, S(0) == 0.99) @constraint(model, I(0) == 0.01) @constraint(model, C(0) == 0.0) if vaccination @variable(model, 0 <= v <= vmax, Infinite(t), start = 0.0) @constraint(model, deriv(S, t) == -(1 - u)*βc*S*I - v*S) @constraint(model, integral(v, t) <= supply) constant_over_collocation(v, t) else @constraint(model, deriv(S, t) == -(1 - u)*βc*S*I) end @constraint(model, deriv(I, t) == (1 - u)*βc*S*I - γ*I) @constraint(model, deriv(C, t) == (1 - u)*βc*S*I) @constraint(model, integral(u, t) <= budget) capacity === nothing || @constraint(model, I <= capacity) @objective(model, Min, C(tf) + 1e-3*integral(u^2, t)) constant_over_collocation(u, t) optimize!(model) solved = has_values(model) grid = supports(t) control = solved ? value.(u) : Float64[] # Collocation supports are not uniformly spaced, so integrate on the actual grid. used = solved ? sum((grid[i+1] - grid[i])*(control[i+1] + control[i])/2 for i in 1:length(grid)-1) : NaN return (; model, t, status = termination_status(model), budget_used = used, final_cases = solved ? value(C(tf)) : NaN, peak_prevalence = solved ? maximum(value.(I)) : NaN, times = supports(t), S = solved ? value.(S) : Float64[], I = solved ? value.(I) : Float64[], u = solved ? value.(u) : Float64[], v = (vaccination && solved) ? value.(model[:v]) : Float64[]) end baseline = control_problem() (status = baseline.status, final_cases = round(baseline.final_cases; digits = 4), peak_prevalence = round(baseline.peak_prevalence; digits = 4)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ****************************************************************************** This program contains Ipopt, a library for large-scale nonlinear optimization. Ipopt is released as open source code under the Eclipse Public License (EPL). For more information visit https://github.com/coin-or/Ipopt ****************************************************************************** ``` ::: ::: {#code-ch14-builder .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (status = LOCALLY_SOLVED, final_cases = 0.4213, peak_prevalence = 0.1311) ``` ::: ::: ### Capacity as a path constraint @eq-ch14-path is enforced at every support rather than only at $t_f$. Whether it changes anything depends on what the unconstrained optimum already does. ::: {#cell-code-ch14-capacity .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} generous = control_problem(; budget = 6.0, umax = 0.8) slack = control_problem(; budget = 6.0, umax = 0.8, capacity = 0.06) binding = control_problem(; budget = 6.0, umax = 0.8, capacity = 0.04) starved = control_problem(; budget = 2.0, capacity = 0.04) [(label = "no cap", status = generous.status, final_cases = round(generous.final_cases; digits = 4), peak = round(generous.peak_prevalence; digits = 4)), (label = "cap 0.06, slack", status = slack.status, final_cases = round(slack.final_cases; digits = 4), peak = round(slack.peak_prevalence; digits = 4)), (label = "cap 0.04, binding", status = binding.status, final_cases = round(binding.final_cases; digits = 4), peak = round(binding.peak_prevalence; digits = 4)), (label = "cap 0.04, budget 2", status = starved.status, final_cases = round(starved.final_cases; digits = 4), peak = round(starved.peak_prevalence; digits = 4))] ``` ::: {#code-ch14-capacity .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 4-element Vector{@NamedTuple{label::String, status::TerminationStatusCode, final_cases::Float64, peak::Float64}}: (label = "no cap", status = LOCALLY_SOLVED, final_cases = 0.128, peak = 0.0531) (label = "cap 0.06, slack", status = LOCALLY_SOLVED, final_cases = 0.128, peak = 0.0531) (label = "cap 0.04, binding", status = LOCALLY_SOLVED, final_cases = 0.1738, peak = 0.04) (label = "cap 0.04, budget 2", status = LOCALLY_INFEASIBLE, final_cases = 0.1002, peak = 0.04) ``` ::: ::: Three regimes, and the distinction between them is the practical content of this section. With a cap of 0.06 the constraint is **slack**: the case-minimising policy already keeps prevalence below it, so adding the constraint changes nothing. At 0.04 it **binds**, the peak sits exactly on the cap — and final cases *rise*. Holding the peak down means spending control early, when suppression buys less total reduction, so a capacity constraint is not free: it is paid for in cases. With a budget of 2.0 the same cap is **infeasible**; no admissible policy can hold prevalence that low for twenty days, and the solver says so rather than returning a misleadingly plausible answer. ### Two controls Vaccination removes susceptibles permanently, so a unit of it is worth more late in an epidemic than a unit of transmission reduction, which lapses the moment it stops. ::: {#cell-code-ch14-vaccination .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} vaccinated = control_problem(; vaccination = true) (status = vaccinated.status, final_cases = round(vaccinated.final_cases; digits = 4), peak_prevalence = round(vaccinated.peak_prevalence; digits = 4), reduction_versus_baseline = round(1 - vaccinated.final_cases/baseline.final_cases; digits = 3)) ``` ::: {#code-ch14-vaccination .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (status = LOCALLY_SOLVED, final_cases = 0.1003, peak_prevalence = 0.0269, reduction_versus_baseline = 0.762) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-ch14-policies .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} figure = Figure(size = (920, 380)) axis1 = Axis(figure[1, 1], xlabel = "Time", ylabel = "Prevalence I(t)") lines!(axis1, baseline.times, baseline.I; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 2, label = "Minimise cases") lines!(axis1, binding.times, binding.I; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 2, label = "Capacity cap 0.04") lines!(axis1, vaccinated.times, vaccinated.I; color = :seagreen, linewidth = 2, label = "With vaccination") hlines!(axis1, [0.04]; color = :grey, linestyle = :dash) axislegend(axis1; position = :rt, framevisible = false) axis2 = Axis(figure[1, 2], xlabel = "Time", ylabel = "Control u(t)") lines!(axis2, baseline.times, baseline.u; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 2, label = "Minimise cases") lines!(axis2, binding.times, binding.u; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 2, label = "Capacity cap 0.04") lines!(axis2, vaccinated.times, vaccinated.u; color = :seagreen, linewidth = 2, label = "With vaccination") axislegend(axis2; position = :rt, framevisible = false) figure ``` ::: {#fig-ch14-policies .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Optimal policies and the trajectories they produce. Left: prevalence under the case-minimising policy, under a binding capacity cap, and with vaccination added. Right: the corresponding non-pharmaceutical control, showing that a capacity constraint pulls control earlier while vaccination substitutes for it. ::: ::: ## Validation An optimiser returning a number is not evidence that the number is right. Three checks apply here. ::: {#cell-code-ch14-validation .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} # 1. The optimiser must respect the constraints it was given. # 2. A control of zero must reproduce the uncontrolled epidemic. uncontrolled = control_problem(; umax = 1e-9) # 3. Refining the collocation grid must not move the answer much. refined = control_problem(; n_supports = 81) (budget_used = round(baseline.budget_used; digits = 4), budget_respected = baseline.budget_used <= 2.0 + 1e-6, uncontrolled_final_cases = round(uncontrolled.final_cases; digits = 4), controlled_final_cases = round(baseline.final_cases; digits = 4), coarse_grid = round(baseline.final_cases; digits = 4), fine_grid = round(refined.final_cases; digits = 4), grid_sensitivity = round(abs(refined.final_cases - baseline.final_cases); digits = 5)) ``` ::: {#code-ch14-validation .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (budget_used = 2.0, budget_respected = true, uncontrolled_final_cases = 0.5835, controlled_final_cases = 0.4213, coarse_grid = 0.4213, fine_grid = 0.4159, grid_sensitivity = 0.0054) ``` ::: ::: The budget holds, forbidding control reproduces a substantially larger epidemic, and doubling the number of supports moves the objective only slightly — so the answer is a property of the problem rather than of the discretisation. The last check is the one most often skipped, and the one that catches a transcription that is too coarse to represent the policy it is asked to find. ## Interpretation and limitations The shape of the optimal policy carries more information than its objective value. Under a pure case-minimising objective with a limited budget, control is deployed in a concentrated burst near the peak, where each unit of transmission reduction averts most infections. Under a capacity constraint it is spread earlier and more thinly, because the binding requirement is no longer total cases but never exceeding the threshold. Those are different policies arising from different stated aims, and neither is "the" optimum. The limitations are worth stating plainly. Ipopt returns **local** solutions: `LOCALLY_SOLVED` means a point satisfying first-order conditions, not a global optimum, and a nonconvex problem may have others. The model is deterministic, so the policy is computed with perfect foresight of a trajectory that no real outbreak provides — a genuinely useful policy must be recomputed as data arrive, which is closer to model predictive control than to a single open-loop solve. The objective encodes only what is written down: minimising cases with a quadratic penalty says nothing about the distribution of harm, the economic cost of lockdown, or adherence. And the regulariser is a numerical convenience whose weight is a modelling choice; making it large enough to matter changes the problem being solved. ## Exercises ### Exercise 1 {#ch14-ex1} Vary the capacity threshold in @eq-ch14-path across a range spanning the slack, binding and infeasible regimes at fixed budget, and plot final cumulative cases against the threshold. Identify the value at which the constraint begins to bind and the value at which the problem becomes infeasible, and explain why the curve is flat on one side of the first and rising on the other. ### Exercise 2 {#ch14-ex2} With both controls active, halve the vaccine supply $V$ while doubling the non-pharmaceutical budget $B$. Report the final cumulative cases and describe how the timing of the two controls changes relative to each other. Explain which control the optimiser prefers to spend first, in terms of the difference between removing susceptibles permanently and suppressing transmission temporarily. ## Companion materials - [Slides](../slides/chapters/14-advanced-optimal-control.html) - [Pluto preview](../notebook-exports/chapters/14-advanced-optimal-control.html) - [Pluto source](../notebooks/chapters/14-advanced-optimal-control.jl)
